# Additional recommended reading

**Why this section exists**

These readings and websites give helpful background, examples, and visual inspiration. None are required, but all are useful if you want to go deeper.

## Books

- Beckerman, A. P., Childs, D. Z., & Petchey, O. L. (2017). *Getting Started with R: An Introduction for Biologists* (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press. The course textbook: the Schedule lists the relevant chapter for each session.
- Wickham, H., Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Grolemund, G. (2023). *R for Data Science* (2nd ed.). O'Reilly. Free online at [https://r4ds.hadley.nz](https://r4ds.hadley.nz). Uses the same `dplyr` and `ggplot2` tools as the data wrangling and data visualisation parts of this book (it writes pipes as `|>`, which works the same as `%>%`; see *Tips and tricks*).
- Childs, D. Z., et al. *APS 240: Data Analysis and Statistics with R*. University of Sheffield. Free online at [https://dzchilds.github.io/stats-for-bio/](https://dzchilds.github.io/stats-for-bio/). A course book that inspired parts of this one, with more detail on the statistics.

## Papers and chapters

- Broman, K. W., & Woo, K. H. (2018). Data organization in spreadsheets. *The American Statistician*, 72(1), 2–10. [https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989). Practical rules for entering and storing data so that it is easy to analyse later (goes with the *Data management* lecture).
- Gotelli, N. J., & Ellison, A. M. (2013). Chapter 4, *Framing and Testing Hypotheses*, in *A Primer of Ecological Statistics* (2nd ed.). Sinauer. Background for the *Hypotheses and questions* lecture.
- Petchey, O., Beckerman, A., & Childs, D. (2009). Shock and awe by statistical software — why R? *Bulletin of the British Ecological Society*, 40(4), 55–58. Why biologists use R rather than point-and-click software (goes with the *Overview and philosophy* lecture).
- Weissgerber, T. L., Milic, N. M., Winham, S. J., & Garovic, V. D. (2015). Beyond bar and line graphs: time for a new data presentation paradigm. *PLoS Biology*, 13(4), e1002128. [https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002128](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002128). Why you should show the data, not just bars of means (goes with *Visualising data with ggplot2* and *Distributions and summarising data*).
- Wickham, H. (2014). Tidy data. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 59(10), 1–23. [https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10). The idea behind the data layout used throughout this book (goes with *Data wrangling with dplyr* and *Combining data sets*).

## Useful websites

- The R Graph Gallery: [https://www.r-graph-gallery.com/](https://www.r-graph-gallery.com/)
- Datanovia ggplot2 tutorials: [https://www.datanovia.com/learn/data-visualization/ggplot2/](https://www.datanovia.com/learn/data-visualization/ggplot2/)
- Datanovia R foundations: [https://www.datanovia.com/learn/programming/r-foundations/](https://www.datanovia.com/learn/programming/r-foundations/)

**Tip:** Pick one reading and one website and spend 30 minutes exploring. A little browsing goes a long way.
